title: Observe before you interpret
description: Separate visible facts from guesses, then choose a respectful follow-up.

steps.title: Establish a baseline
steps.caption: Listen to an ordinary, neutral exchange before interpreting a later change.
steps.coach: In the fictional scene, the participant answers a neutral question at their usual pace. Compare this person with their own baseline rather than with a universal body-language rule.
steps.alt: Two people converse. A baseline timeline appears before a later four-second pause.

steps.title: Record the visible fact
steps.caption: A four-second pause is observable. Its cause is still unknown.
steps.coach: Write exactly what happened: the participant paused, looked twice at an object, or changed a word. Avoid labels such as guilty, dishonest or traumatised.
steps.alt: The later reply includes a four-second pause. The fact card records the pause without assigning a motive.

steps.title: Keep alternatives open
steps.caption: The same pause could reflect memory search, uncertainty or distraction.
steps.coach: Generate at least two possible explanations. None becomes a fact because it sounds plausible. This exercise uses fictional behaviour and cannot diagnose real people.
steps.alt: An observed pause connects to a hypothesis card and a respectful follow-up question. The caption also notes distraction as an alternative.

steps.title: Ask one useful question
steps.caption: Use the observation to guide a question, and leave room for correction.
steps.coach: Try: You paused before answering; was the choice difficult? Let the participant disagree or offer another explanation. A respectful question is more useful than an accusation.
steps.alt: An open question follows the fact and several hypotheses. The participant can clarify or decline.

steps.title: Practise fact versus inference
steps.caption: Classify each statement, then read why it belongs in that category.
steps.coach: In Practice, sort six statements into observation or interpretation. The goal is precise language, not an ability to detect lies from gestures.
steps.alt: Fact, hypotheses and follow-up cards distinguish a recorded pause from possible motives and a question.

title: Measure a force honestly
description: Log rehearsal choices and practise a confident response to both hits and misses.

steps.title: Name the target
steps.caption: Choose Circle as this rehearsal target before giving the instruction.
steps.coach: This example compares Circle, Triangle and Square. It is a small demonstration universe, not a proven psychological force. Define the target before collecting responses.
steps.alt: Circle, Triangle and Square are shown, with Circle marked as the rehearsal target.

steps.title: Keep wording consistent
steps.caption: Use one short instruction and accept the participant's first genuine choice.
steps.coach: Write your exact wording and keep the language and setting consistent during a batch. Do not secretly change the target after hearing the answer.
steps.alt: One instruction sits above three available shapes. The participant can select any of them.

steps.title: Record every response
steps.caption: A hit is Circle. Triangle and Square are misses for this target.
steps.coach: Practice lets you enter observed rehearsal choices. The counters start at zero, store only this session, and never invent successful trials. Undo corrects an accidental entry.
steps.alt: An example trial tally separates target hits from all other choices. Example data is explicitly labelled.

steps.title: Rehearse the miss path
steps.caption: Acknowledge a miss and use the alternate ending prepared before the choice.
steps.coach: Do not blame the participant or relabel an ordinary miss as proof of influence. Rehearse a clean transition just as carefully as the exact-hit reveal.
steps.alt: Two branches follow the response: reveal on a hit, acknowledge and transition on a miss.

steps.title: Review the batch
steps.caption: A session percentage describes those trials; it does not guarantee the next result.
steps.coach: The suggested first batch is twenty trials. Small samples and changing conditions limit conclusions. Compare similar conditions before revising your script.
steps.alt: A hit-rate bar is labelled example data, with a reminder that observed results do not guarantee future choices.

title: Build a drawing reveal in layers
description: Reveal orientation and geometry before the exact object, using three original practice drawings.

steps.title: Set a simple drawing rule
steps.caption: Use one recognisable object, without words, numbers or a complex scene.
steps.coach: The coaching example is a simple house. The target is openly known in this training exercise. It does not demonstrate a secret glimpse or a proprietary gimmick.
steps.alt: A simple house outline is shown as an openly known training target.

steps.title: Start with orientation
steps.caption: Describe the overall spread before naming the object.
steps.coach: For this house drawing, begin with a shape that is wider than it is tall. If the participant's actual drawing differs, use its real properties instead.
steps.alt: A width guide surrounds the house drawing to show its broad orientation.

steps.title: Add geometry
steps.caption: Notice straight edges and a triangular feature above a rectangular body.
steps.coach: Give structural information one piece at a time. Geometry is more specific than orientation but still leaves several possibilities open.
steps.alt: The roof triangle and rectangular body are highlighted separately.

steps.title: Reveal the distinguishing detail
steps.caption: Move from a manufactured object to a doorway beneath the roof.
steps.coach: A doorway helps the participant recognise the intended house. Pause for recognition; do not pressure someone to agree with a weak resemblance.
steps.alt: A door is added beneath the triangular roof, making the rough house recognisable.

steps.title: Compare at the climax
steps.caption: Name the house only after its structural features have been revealed.
steps.coach: In Practice, switch between House, Tree and Boat and reveal their clue ladders one beat at a time. The drawings are original teaching examples.
steps.alt: A completed rough house drawing sits beside its clue ladder, ending in the exact name.

title: Map the prediction before the choice
description: Inspect three prepared outcomes and rehearse their retrieval routes.

steps.title: Define the remembered effect
steps.caption: Write one clear theatrical event and decide what commitment the audience will remember.
steps.coach: Our teaching model uses three prepared envelopes. It openly shows the training method; it does not claim that one fixed prediction covers every free choice.
steps.alt: Three envelopes A, B and C are visibly prepared before any rehearsal choice.

steps.title: Prepare every outcome
steps.caption: Envelope A contains Key, B contains Coin, and C contains Stone.
steps.coach: Check each outcome and its location before performing. This index is a conceptual model, not a demonstration of concealed physical handling.
steps.alt: The three training envelopes are paired with Key, Coin and Stone respectively.

steps.title: Make and accept the choice
steps.caption: Let the participant choose an object, then follow its already prepared route.
steps.coach: Do not change the participant's answer to protect the script. In Practice, select any object and inspect the matching envelope route.
steps.alt: A Coin choice activates the preconfigured route to envelope B.

steps.title: Reveal from broad to exact
steps.caption: Keep the retrieval calm, then let the specific match be the strongest detail.
steps.coach: A real routine needs natural handling and an honest theatrical premise. Do not make a claim of inaccessible commitment that your actual presentation fails to establish.
steps.alt: The highlighted Coin route reaches envelope B, whose prepared Coin card is revealed.

steps.title: Rehearse all routes
steps.caption: Reset the three envelopes and practise Key, Coin and Stone in mixed order.
steps.coach: Performer view exposes all contents for training. Audience view hides the training index until a reveal. Changing the view does not change the prepared outcome mapping.
steps.alt: All three fixed outcome routes are displayed for rehearsal and reset.

title: Reveal a word through meaning
description: Use original practice text and build a semantic clue ladder without letter fishing.

steps.title: Use a clear reading procedure
steps.caption: Open, look at one word, close, and concentrate. Keep instructions short.
steps.coach: This training page is original text. The selected word is openly known to you in Practice; the activity teaches reveal structure, not a secret acquisition method.
steps.alt: An original open-book practice page contains the words Lantern, Forest and Rocket.

steps.title: Begin with an image
steps.caption: For Lantern, start with a small source of light in a dark place.
steps.coach: A semantic image introduces meaning without jumping immediately to the word. Choose properties that actually fit the selected word.
steps.alt: A lantern illustration glows softly beside the practice page.

steps.title: Narrow the category
steps.caption: Move to a portable, manufactured object rather than a living thing.
steps.coach: Category is a second layer. Keep it distinct from the first clue and avoid a long series of questions that asks the participant to supply the answer.
steps.alt: The Lantern clue ladder advances from light to a portable manufactured object.

steps.title: Add a distinctive feature
steps.caption: A protective frame and a handle make the image more specific.
steps.coach: Progress toward the distinctive feature before the exact identity. If you use a different word, prepare a different clue ladder instead of forcing these clues to fit.
steps.alt: A handle and protective lantern frame are highlighted as distinguishing details.

steps.title: Name and confirm the word
steps.caption: End with Lantern, then ask the participant to confirm what they selected.
steps.coach: Practice includes original clue ladders for Lantern, Forest and Rocket. Reset before changing the training word. No private text or proprietary book-test design is used.
steps.alt: The clue ladder finishes at Lantern with one final confirmation.

title: Design one impossible moment
description: Choose an effect, keep its essential conditions, and remove unnecessary procedure.

steps.title: State the effect first
steps.caption: The audience remembers an impossible event rather than your secret mechanics.
steps.coach: Our example sentence is: A visible prediction matches the participant's chosen object. Build the procedure around that event before adding moves.
steps.alt: Commit, Choose and Reveal form a three-beat timeline, with repeated displays beneath it.

steps.title: Choose one clear condition
steps.caption: Introduce the prediction early and establish one meaningful condition.
steps.coach: One visible condition can help the audience follow the premise. Do not repeatedly prove fairness when the extra actions only lengthen the procedure.
steps.alt: The prediction is introduced and placed in view before the choice.

steps.title: Identify likely explanations
steps.caption: Ask what an audience might reasonably suspect, then design a motivated convincer.
steps.coach: Separate a suspected explanation from proof that it occurred. A condition has value when the real routine actually establishes it.
steps.alt: The three-beat timeline is compared with repeated displays and inspections that may add no meaningful condition.

steps.title: Trim the procedure
steps.caption: Keep commitment, choice and reveal. Cut repetitions that add no new condition.
steps.coach: Practice presents six action cards. Keep the three essential beats of this example and remove the three repeated displays. Another routine may need a different structure.
steps.alt: Repeated displays, inspections and explanations are crossed out while commitment, choice and reveal remain.

steps.title: Check the remembered event
steps.caption: Ask a test viewer what happened after a short delay.
steps.coach: A concise routine is successful when its conditions and climax are understandable. Do not infer audience memory from your own knowledge of the method.
steps.alt: The final timeline contains three clear beats and ends with an audience memory question.

title: Place movement on a motivated beat
description: Compare audience focus across a display, question and reveal.

steps.title: Locate the important moment
steps.caption: During a prop display, the object is the audience's main point of interest.
steps.coach: The attention cone is a coaching model, not an eye-tracking measurement. Avoid assuming that all spectators look in the same direction.
steps.alt: Two audience figures face a displayed card, marked as the current focus of interest.

steps.title: Give the movement a reason
steps.caption: Clearing space or handing over a pen should have an understandable purpose.
steps.coach: Rehearse the ordinary reason for an action. A gesture that only exists to hide another gesture can make the handling feel contrived.
steps.alt: The tabletop diagram labels Display, Pen handover and Reveal as different beats; arrows show coaching focus.

steps.title: Compare the question beat
steps.caption: A meaningful question can shift interest toward the participant and their answer.
steps.coach: This is a possible conversational offbeat, not guaranteed concealment. Keep your eyes, speech and hand speed consistent and accept that someone may still watch the props.
steps.alt: Arrows direct the coaching focus toward the figure at the question beat rather than the displayed card.

steps.title: Keep the reveal clean
steps.caption: At the reveal, attention returns to the impossible result.
steps.coach: Do not place unrelated handling over the climax. Let the audience register the result. This lesson visualises timing without teaching a physical switch.
steps.alt: The revealed prediction becomes the focus while the other objects remain still.

steps.title: Choose and review a beat
steps.caption: Select a rehearsal beat and read its timing tradeoff.
steps.coach: Practice compares three plausible moments and shows why a motivated question can be useful. Film your own lawful performance from spectator eye level to test the real handling.
steps.alt: Display, question and reveal are arranged on a timing strip for comparison.

title: Arrange and compare symbol rows
description: Rehearse clear matching displays with five simple geometric symbols.

steps.title: Learn a clear symbol set
steps.caption: Use Circle, Triangle, Twin bars, Three dots and Wave.
steps.coach: These geometric drawings are original assets for the app. Each symbol has a spoken label so the exercise remains usable without relying only on colour.
steps.alt: Five original geometric teaching symbols appear in a labelled row.

steps.title: Separate the two rows
steps.caption: Place one row for the performer and another for the participant.
steps.coach: Keep the spacing and orientation consistent. A clear display lets a spectator understand which positions are being compared.
steps.alt: Two labelled symbol rows use the same five positions.

steps.title: Change one arrangement
steps.caption: Swap two pairs in the participant row and compare matching positions.
steps.coach: Practice lets you swap cards or rotate a known row deterministically. It does not secretly force a choice and does not generate evidence of ESP.
steps.alt: Twin bars and Triangle exchange positions, as do Three dots and Wave. Circle remains in the first position.

steps.title: Reveal the comparison
steps.caption: Count only identical symbols in the same position.
steps.coach: Practice hides the comparison until you request it. A mismatch is still a mismatch; the app never changes a symbol after the arrangement is chosen.
steps.alt: Lines connect only symbols that match in both shape and position.

steps.title: Plan an escalating routine
steps.caption: Move from a simple match to participant agency, then a prepared final prediction.
steps.coach: The arrangement board rehearses display clarity. A complete performance still needs an original method and a coherent theatrical premise, without scientific psychic claims.
steps.alt: Two aligned symbol rows illustrate a clear visible match; the caption describes an escalating performance sequence.

title: Separate hypnosis from its myths
description: Sort explanations while keeping agency and variable responses visible.

steps.title: Use a modest working model
steps.caption: Attention, imagination and response to suggestion form a useful educational model.
steps.coach: This diagram explains concepts. It does not assess susceptibility or guide an induction. There are different theories about how hypnotic responses arise.
steps.alt: Attention, imagination and suggestion are drawn as three linked concept cards.

steps.title: Keep agency visible
steps.caption: Participation is voluntary, and a request to stop ends the activity.
steps.coach: Avoid a controller-versus-controlled picture. The participant's choices and consent remain part of the interaction.
steps.alt: A participant figure remains connected to a clearly marked Stop control.

steps.title: Allow variable responses
steps.caption: People and suggestions differ; one response does not predict every other response.
steps.coach: Never rank someone's intelligence, worth or honesty from a response. A quiet or absent response is information to accept rather than a failure to shame.
steps.alt: Different response bars are shown without ranking people or assigning personality traits.

steps.title: Correct the overclaims
steps.caption: Hypnosis does not establish truth, guaranteed obedience or reliable recovered memories.
steps.coach: Keep this app's demonstrations educational and non-clinical. Do not use hypnosis to claim proof of a private event or to make treatment promises.
steps.alt: Truth detection, guaranteed obedience and memory proof are marked as unsupported claims.

steps.title: Practise careful explanations
steps.caption: Sort six statements into a careful model or an overclaim.
steps.coach: Read the explanation after each answer. The linked professional sources discuss the general model and myths; this sorting activity is original course practice.
steps.alt: Attention, Imagination and Suggestion cards sit beside a participant and Stop control, with a reminder about agency and variable responses.

title: Rehearse a short pre-talk
description: Choose words that explain the activity, preserve agency, and check consent.

steps.title: Ask what they expect
steps.caption: Begin with an open question about the participant's understanding.
steps.coach: Try: What do you expect this to feel like? Listen rather than argue. This is a fictional conversation rehearsal, with no induction or clinical screening.
steps.alt: Four pre-talk principle cards cover explanation, agency, variation and consent. The caption recommends an open question.

steps.title: Explain the limited goal
steps.caption: Describe a voluntary attention-and-imagination demonstration in ordinary language.
steps.coach: Do not promise treatment, truth detection or total control. Explain only what the planned educational activity actually involves.
steps.alt: A short explanation connects attention and imagination to a clearly limited demonstration.

steps.title: Make stopping easy
steps.caption: Agree a stop signal and say that changing their mind is acceptable.
steps.coach: A stop signal is useful only when you act on it immediately. Do not treat agreement to this explanation as agreement to filming or a different activity.
steps.alt: The Confirm agency card is highlighted and says Stop at any time, beside the other pre-talk principles.

steps.title: Remove performance pressure
steps.caption: Invite honest feedback and allow small, different or absent responses.
steps.coach: Avoid statements that only intelligent or cooperative people succeed. Such praise can pressure a person to report something they did not experience.
steps.alt: The Accept variation principle is highlighted with the phrase Honest feedback is welcome.

steps.title: Check consent before proceeding
steps.caption: Ask whether they want to try the specific activity, and accept yes, no or uncertainty.
steps.coach: In Practice, answer four fictional objections. Read feedback and review all four principles before taking any real-world next step.
steps.alt: A consent check follows explanation, agency and acceptance of variable responses.
